content.p: Ray O'Connor, known as "Rocky", spent about a quarter of a century in the Western Australian Parliament, served as a minister under two premiers and led the state for a single year, from 1982 to 1983. He is remembered less for any of that than for two things that followed. In 1995 he was convicted of stealing a $25,000 Bond Corporation cheque, a case that grew out of the WA Inc royal commission, and he went to jail. And his name became attached, through rumour and then through sworn testimony, to the unsolved 1975 murder of the Perth brothel madam Shirley Finn, for which he was police minister at the time.

The two stories have very different standing. The first was tested by a royal commission and a court. The second was tested by a coroner, who found that none of the evidence against O'Connor came close to the standard needed to say he was involved. O'Connor consistently denied any link to Finn, and a friend told his funeral that he always maintained his innocence of the theft as well.

O'Connor was the son of a policeman, according to The West Australian. He was first elected to Parliament in 1959 and served as a minister under both Sir David Brand and Sir Charles Court. The ABC described him as a talented footballer and small business owner who became a long-serving Liberal minister in the 1960s and 1970s. The Premier of the day, Colin Barnett, listed the portfolios he held: labour and industry, consumer affairs, immigration, fisheries and environment, transport, and police.

In his valedictory speech to the Assembly on 23 August 1984 O'Connor said he had been in Parliament for 26 years and had handled 18 portfolios. Obituaries from the ABC and The West Australian gave 24 years; a second West Australian report spoke of 25. The difference is not explained on the pages and may reflect how the years are counted.

He took over from Court in 1982 when Court resigned, and lasted a year. Labor's Brian Burke won the 1983 election. The political analyst Peter Kennedy told the ABC that O'Connor was an old-style politician who was unlucky to reach the top late in his career, when Labor was resurgent under a "new broom" in Burke and Malcolm Bryce, and "wasn't really any match for it". Curtin University's David Black said the single year as premier did not reflect a contribution to state politics that was "very considerable". Kennedy added that controversy dogged him throughout his career.

The conviction has its roots in an early-1980s development. Bond Corporation wanted approval from the City of Stirling for Observation City, a large beachfront hotel and apartment project at Scarborough. The royal commission, whose report on the matter ran to chapter 23 of its sixth volume, found that Bond became anxious early in 1984 that the council might refuse the proposal or attach impossible conditions. The company engaged O'Connor, by then a former premier, to lobby councillors whose sympathies lay with the Liberal Party. Mr Buckley, the Bond manager concerned with the project, told the commission he felt at the time that O'Connor had made no useful contribution to the approval. Alan Bond told the commission he recalled that O'Connor was paid $50,000.

On 18 April 1984 a Bond Corporation cheque for $25,000 was drawn to "Cash — Mt Lawley Campaign Fund" and sent to Bond's consultant Jack Walsh with a memorandum saying, "As arranged with Peter Beckwith, yourself and myself, I am enclosing a cheque for you to distribute." The commission accepted that those last words suggested the money was meant to go to more than one person. It was negotiated the next day.

The commission found that a $25,000 deposit went into O'Connor's own account at the R&I Bank's Town Hall branch in Perth on 19 April, the day the cheque was negotiated. It noted that the account was then overdrawn by $95,651, that this was the first deposit since 28 December 1983, and that O'Connor had a tax liability of $27,069, for which he had drawn a cheque on 14 April that was not debited until 24 April. O'Connor denied his account needed money. The commissioners disagreed, and recorded that he had been given every opportunity to explain the deposit "but was unable to do so in any believable way". The bank had destroyed the records that would have identified the account into which the cheque was paid, in line with its policy, which the commission called unfortunate.
The commission also heard from Liberal Party figures, including George Cash, that the party never received the money. Buckley said he had "no doubt" the cheque was meant for O'Connor.

A second thread was a secret tape. In March 1987, O'Connor visited the Premier, Brian Burke, in his Parliament House office. By O'Connor's own evidence, Burke asked whether he knew anything about $30,000 said to have been paid to Cash, and O'Connor answered "sure; I did". He told the commission that this was not true and that he had been trying to draw out what Burke knew about Cash.

On 2 April 1987, in the electoral office of Burke's brother Terry, O'Connor was recorded without his knowledge. In essence, the commission said, he stated or agreed that he had received $30,000 in $50 notes from Beckwith and had handed it to Cash, then a Stirling councillor, in return for the council approving the application. He suspected towards the end that he was being taped.

The commission did not take the tape at its word. It heard from ten of the 13 councillors, examined their finances and scrutinised Cash's in particular, and found "no evidence whatsoever" that Cash or any councillor received illicit money over Observation City. Neither O'Connor's recorded statements nor the Bond memoranda, it said, could prove a receipt by any councillor. It also found no evidence of misconduct by Cash involving a Mr Joe Scarfo, a matter raised during the hearings.

The commission found that the $25,000 cheque was delivered "in pursuance of a corrupt arrangement made earlier" and that Bond Corporation intended it to be distributed to councillors who, the company had been led to believe by O'Connor, had been swayed by the promise of reward. It summarised his misconduct in four parts: fostering a false belief in Walsh and Bond that a cost was involved in securing council approval; receiving the cheque for that purpose; using the proceeds for his own purposes; and publishing statements in March and April 1987 capable of damaging the reputation of other people. The word it used was "improperly". It could not say whether anyone else still living was party to the conduct, noting that the deaths of Walsh and Beckwith had cost it important evidence.
It also found the conduct of the Burke brothers over the secret recording, and their failure afterwards to tell the Commissioner of Police, to be improper.

Elsewhere in the same chapter the commissioners described O'Connor's business after he quit Parliament. He gave his farewell speech in August 1984. The Ray O'Connor Consultancy began on 1 July 1984, and Laurie Connell recalled an agreement that finance would be made available to help O'Connor set up his business once he left Parliament. O'Connor's America's Cup Festival of Sport later won state funding exceeding $700,000, and he agreed that he "owed the Burkes a favour" for government support. The commission said that by early 1987 he had become a provider of miscellaneous information to Burke about the Liberal opposition.

The pages available give the outcome rather than the trial. The ABC said O'Connor was convicted of stealing the $25,000 Bond cheque and spent six months in jail; The West Australian said he was jailed for fraud in 1995 in the wake of WA Inc, and later that he was jailed for six months for stealing the cheque. Other ABC reports described the conviction as one for fraud. The sources do not give the length of the sentence handed down as distinct from time served, so the six-month figure is the one the reports repeat.

On his release he rejected the verdict. According to The West Australian he said: "The crime for which I was convicted never occurred. How can you have remorse?" He added that a politician or ex-politician of high prominence had little chance of escaping conviction, innocent or not. Max Healy, who was held at Wooroloo prison farm a week apart from him, told the Finn inquest that O'Connor was upset by the allegations about Finn, but nothing in the pages shows him changing his position on the cheque.

Shirley Finn, a well-known socialite and brothel owner, was found shot four times in the head, slumped in her white Dodge Phoenix beside Royal Perth Golf Course on the morning of 23 June 1975, wearing a full-length ball gown. She had been due at a tax hearing two days later, and was said to have threatened to expose illicit dealings by politicians, businessmen and police. O'Connor was police minister. In 2010, The West Australian reported, he told the paper's reporters he had no connection with the shooting.

The allegation resurfaced publicly in 2017 when Finn's former driver, Leigh Beswick, told ABC's Australian Story that Finn and O'Connor had an affair, and that she overheard Finn tell him, "if I go down you go down". O'Connor had consistently denied having met Finn and called the suggestion a joke. Beswick told the inquest she believed Detective Don Hancock had shot Finn as a favour to O'Connor; her account of who fired the shots rested on what an ex-boyfriend, a detective, told her in 2004.

Other evidence cut the other way. Max Healy, who knew O'Connor from football and met him again in prison, testified that O'Connor said he had never met Finn and was upset about rumours that he had fixed her tax problem. Healy said O'Connor told him an internal police investigation had found that Vice Squad chief Bernie Johnson had stolen from police custody the rifle used in the killing. A former officer, Colynn Rowe, said he had seen photograph albums at Finn's house after her death in which he recognised O'Connor among party guests, but the ABC noted that, so far, all the evidence linking O'Connor to Finn was hearsay, and that the albums could not be found. A taxi driver, Ray Gardner, told the court he saw O'Connor shoot Finn; the coroner said he had great difficulty giving the evidence any weight, and The West Australian reported that aspects of it, such as a claim of clear sunny weather, did not fit the wet morning.

The coroner also queried the tax-threat theory. A threat made over a tax debt in 1973 or early 1974, he observed, was hard to connect with a killing 18 months later, and as a state politician O'Connor had no authority over the Commonwealth Taxation Department. A public servant's account, relayed through an author's interview notes, that Johnson and three others visited O'Connor's office two days before the murder was recorded but described by the coroner only as possible support.

Coroner Barry King delivered his findings in August 2020 after hearing from almost 70 witnesses over 27 days. He could not say who killed Finn, and did not find that any person on his shortlist was responsible. Of O'Connor he wrote: "Mr O'Connor was clearly a colourful character. There is evidence indicating that he may have been involved with Ms Finn, and weak circumstantial evidence suggesting that he may have procured Ms Finn's death. However, none of that evidence comes close to establishing his involvement to the applicable standard of proof." An earlier police Special Crime Squad review, he noted, also found no direct evidence against O'Connor but could not exclude that he may have procured her death. The Canberra Times reported that the coroner named 11 possible suspects, including O'Connor.
Finn's daughter, Bridget Shewring, said her family had been denied justice. The coroner said the investigation was back in the hands of the WA Police.

O'Connor died in a nursing home in February 2013, surrounded by family, The West Australian reported. His funeral drew Premier Barnett and former Liberal leaders; ex-premier Richard Court attended the cremation. His friend Alan Ridge told mourners he had never doubted O'Connor's innocence of the theft, and described a sharp mind, a head for figures and a boyish humour. The celebrant compared him with Richard III, a figure he said was unfairly maligned.

In December 2023 his grandson Reece O'Connor was one of three men jailed in Perth for trying to take possession of 99 kilograms of methamphetamine, hidden in latex pillows and imported from Thailand. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 13 years and six months.
